name: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
title: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
answer: AI-assisted timekeeping and billing narratives cover the creation, review, and standardization of time entries and invoice descriptions in legal practice. This includes turning raw activity logs, calendar events, emails, and document edits into narrative text that meets client billing guidelines. It also covers auditing existing narratives for compliance, consistency, and defensibility. The work sits within legal operations because it affects revenue, client trust, and matter management. It is not about replacing timekeepers but about reducing the friction of recording work accurately.

sections.body: AI-assisted timekeeping and billing narratives cover the creation, review, and standardization of time entries and invoice descriptions in legal practice. This includes turning raw activity logs, calendar events, emails, and document edits into narrative text that meets client billing guidelines. It also covers auditing existing narratives for compliance, consistency, and defensibility. The work sits within legal operations because it affects revenue, client trust, and matter management. It is not about replacing timekeepers but about reducing the friction of recording work accurately.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on a law firm's existing practice management or time entry platform, often through an API or embedded assistant. They rely on access to structured activity data such as timers, document management logs, and communication metadata. Processing may happen in a cloud environment with role-based access controls, or on premises where client confidentiality demands it. The underlying models are usually general-purpose language models fine-tuned on firm-specific billing language and historical narratives. No special hardware is required beyond standard secure servers or cloud instances.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first collecting signals about a timekeeper's activity during a matter, then mapping those signals to a draft narrative. A language model proposes a description that states what was done, for whom, and why it advanced the matter, using approved task codes and phrasing. Human timekeepers review and edit the draft before it is posted, because the narrative must be accurate and defensible. Some systems also compare drafts against client outside counsel guidelines to flag block billing, vague terms, or disallowed activities. The model learns from accepted corrections to improve future suggestions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on confidentiality, accuracy, and client trust. Billing narratives are attorney work product and often privileged, so any AI processing must respect data boundaries and retention rules. A key risk is that a generated narrative overstates or mischaracterizes work, which can lead to fee disputes or ethical problems. Provenance matters: firms need to know which entries were AI-drafted, which were human-edited, and what source data was used. Client billing guidelines and engagement letters may require disclosure or prohibit certain automated drafting, so governance must track those obligations.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward tighter integration with matter activity feeds, so narratives can be drafted in near real time as work happens. Future systems may compare narratives against matter budgets and historical patterns to flag inefficiencies or potential write-offs before invoices go out. There is also movement toward client-side AI that reviews law firm invoices against the same narrative standards, creating a kind of shared vocabulary. Over time, the distinction between timekeeping, project management, and matter pricing may blur as narratives become structured data rather than free text.
